system: You are a careful software engineer working alone in the current folder.
prompt:
This folder holds `specification.md`, the specification of a binary file format, and three sample files, each a valid file of that format (`.fpk`) with its text form beside it (`.txt`). You have a shell, and you may write and run files in this folder and nowhere else. There is no network.

Your task: write, from this specification alone, in Go, using its standard library only, one program, with a file `run.sh` beside it that runs it as `sh run.sh <mode> <file>` (building it first if it must be built), with three modes.

- `read <file>`: reads a file of the binary format. If it is a valid file by the specification, print its text form (section 8) to standard output exactly, byte for byte, and nothing else. Otherwise print one line that begins `refused:` followed by the reason, and nothing else. Whatever the bytes, the program must answer one of these two ways: never hang, never crash with a traceback, and never use more time or memory than the specification allows a reader (section 6 and section 3.5).
- `name <file>`: reads a text form. If it is a valid text form by the specification, print the content's name (section 3.4) of the binary file it describes, as 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits. Otherwise print one line beginning `refused:` with the reason.
- `graph <file>`: reads a file of the binary format. If it is a valid file, print its graph (section 5) as one JSON value, `{"files":[...]}`, one object a file in path order: `{"path":...,"document":...,"edges":[...],"outbound":[...],"inbound":[...],"documentation":[...],"documentedBy":[...]}`, where `document` is the file's document path, each edge and each documentation item is an object of the members section 5 names, and every member is present or absent by section 5's rules. Whitespace and the order of an object's members are yours to choose. Otherwise print one line beginning `refused:` with the reason.

The specification is your only authority. Wherever it does not tell you enough to write a line of your program, or says two different things, or leans on something you would have to guess or to know from elsewhere (a library, a language, another program), do not guess silently: write the question down in `questions.md`, one question to a heading, each with the section it is about, what is missing or in conflict, and the choice you made. That file is as important as the program.

Test your program on the three samples, and make files of your own that a reader must refuse, to test that it refuses them. When you are done, say in a few lines what you built, how you tested it, and what you are least sure of.

Also write `refusals.md`: every kind of file or text your program refuses, one to a line, each with the section that requires it.
answer:
I've built the program, `questions.md` (20 questions) and `refusals.md`. All three modes work on the samples, and all 171 test checks pass.

**What it is.** About 2,700 lines of Go, standard library only, in `main.go`, `binary.go`, `walker.go` and `textform.go`. `run.sh` builds the binary into this folder when it is missing or older than its sources, then runs it.
- **`read`** follows section 6's steps in order. Nothing is printed until every check has passed, so a refusal never comes after partial output.
- **`graph`** gives the graph by section 5's rules.
- **`name`** turns the text back into the uncompressed sections and runs them through the same checks. It then writes the text again from those sections and compares it with the input byte for byte. That comparison is how wrong member order, duplicate members and any other non-canonical form get refused.

**How I tested it.**
- **Samples:** `read` reproduces all three texts byte for byte. `name` gives the same content name as a separate Python script that reads it from the binary. `graph` gives valid JSON, and I checked the every-fact sample's graph against section 5 by hand.
- **Refusals:** 159 hand-made files and texts are in `tests/binary/` and `tests/text/`, each with the reason it must be refused in `tests/expected.tsv`. Run `sh tests/run_tests.sh` to check them all.
- **Fuzzing:** about 11,000 mutated binaries, with the sections re-hashed so the mutations reach the record checks, and 3,000 mutated texts. None crashed or gave a bad answer, and every binary that was accepted round-tripped through `name`.
- **Larger files:** a separately generated 100,000-file scan, across many 256-file record frames, reads in under a second using 28 MB. A file near the 64× inflation limit gives its 876 MB text in 5 s using 54 MB. The worst case I found for memory was a hostile 21 MB file of 6 million distinct strings: about 330 MB and 7 s.

**What I'm least sure of:**
- **When the text is refused.** Section 3.5 lets a reader refuse the text past a bound but leaves open how to count it. I count a file's path once per line it appears on, not once per record. Otherwise a 30 KB file would require a 500 GB text. So I may refuse a text that the looser reading says must be written (questions 1–2).
- **The graph has no size limit.** The spec always requires the graph, so a small hostile file can produce a very large one (question 3).
- **My guesses on the graph:** that `edges`, `outbound` and `inbound` are always present even when empty; that "qualifiers hold `re-export`" means an exact match; and that a parameter's type edge carries both `from` and `parameter` (questions 4–7).
- **Deflate edge cases** are decided by Go's `compress/flate`. I did not compare them against zlib (question 14).
- **Exit status** is 0 for both output and `refused:`; the task didn't specify one (question 19).

The Python test tools are in `tools/`. The build cache is `.gocache/` (42 MB), and you can delete it.
